title: Internet Official Protocol Standards
summary: A snapshot published by the RFC Editor listing the official protocol standards, best current practice, and experimental RFCs, as of 18 February 2008, that had not been obsoleted. Newly published or changed RFCs were starred. It is not a complete index. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 7100.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of which internet rules were official on one day in 2008. Newer lists have since taken its place.

subtitle: A snapshot of internet standards as of February 2008

tldr.problem: The internet community needs a clear, published list of which protocols are official standards, which are still in development, and which have been superseded or are merely experimental.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5000 publishes a snapshot listing all official Internet standards, draft standards, proposed standards, best current practice documents, and experimental RFCs that were active as of February 18, 2008, organized by their maturity level and assigned standard number.
tldr.outcome: This was a Historic informational document that served as a periodic checkpoint. An up-to-date version is maintained online daily by the RFC Editor, making printed snapshots less necessary. RFC 7100 replaced it.

today: RFC 5000 is marked Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 7100. It serves as a historical record of the internet standards landscape in February 2008. The RFC Editor now maintains a live, daily-updated list of standards at http://www.rfc-editor.org instead of publishing periodic RFC snapshots.

sections.title: What This List Is
sections.content:
RFC 5000 is a catalog of internet protocols and standards published by the RFC Editor in May 2008. It lists every protocol that had official status at that point in time (February 18, 2008), along with protocols and practices still in development or marked as experimental. The document does not include informational or historic RFCs—only those with active status in the standards process.

This RFC obsoletes RFC 3700, which was the previous snapshot. The RFC Editor publishes such snapshots periodically to document the state of standardization at a given moment. New or changed protocols since the previous edition are marked with an asterisk for easy reference.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it as a yearbook showing which internet technologies were official in 2008. It organized them into groups by how mature they were.

sections.title: The Standards Process
sections.content:
Internet standards follow a formal process defined in RFC 2026. Protocols progress through several maturity levels as they develop, gain review, and earn support from the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF).

RFC 5000 lists protocols in their respective maturity categories: Standard Protocols (the most mature, each assigned a unique STD number), Draft Standard Protocols, Proposed Standard Protocols (the most common maturity level), Best Current Practice documents (guidelines rather than protocol specifications), and Experimental Protocols (for exploratory or niche applications). The document also notes protocols that have moved from one level to another since the previous edition.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols don't become official overnight. They start as proposals, get tested and reviewed, and gradually mature into full standards. This list organized them by how far along they were.

sections.title: Accessing the Standards
sections.content:
RFC 5000 points readers to the RFC Editor's online repository at http://www.rfc-editor.org, where individual RFCs can be retrieved by number. At the time of publication, the site maintained an up-to-date version of the standards list at http://www.rfc-editor.org/rfcxx00.html, updated daily with newly published RFCs and status changes.

Each RFC is available online in plain text format. The RFC Editor is the official archive for all RFC documents and maintains indexes, submission procedures, and publication policies. The document notes that this snapshot was not a complete index to all RFCs—it covers only those with active status in the standards process.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC Editor maintains a website where you can find any protocol document. This list was a printable snapshot of a document they update every day.

sections.title: Why It Is Historic
sections.content:
RFC 5000 is now marked Historic, replaced by RFC 7100, for a practical reason: snapshots become outdated quickly. In 2008, printing a comprehensive list was useful for reference and archival. Today, anyone can visit the RFC Editor's website and see the current state of standards in real time, updated daily.

The document itself notes that a live version is maintained daily on the RFC Editor site. As internet standards evolved and publication frequency increased, the need for periodic printed snapshots diminished. The approach of embedding a snapshot in an RFC gave way to living documentation on the web. This document serves as a historical record of the standards landscape in early 2008.
sections.plainLanguage: This list became old-fashioned because now you can just check the RFC Editor website to see the current list whenever you want, instead of waiting for someone to publish a new RFC.

references.text: Bradner, S., "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", BCP 9, RFC 2026, October 1996.
